summary:
Abia is a state in southern Nigeria and stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in full: same-sex sexual acts between men carry up to 14 years' imprisonment under secular law, and entering a same-sex marriage or civil union is punishable by 14 years. Anyone who administers, witnesses, abets or aides the solemnization of such a union, or who supports the registration, operation or sustenance of gay clubs, societies, organisations, processions or meetings, faces 10 years' imprisonment. The Act also punishes public displays of same-sex amorous relationships.

Sharia penal codes do not apply in Abia. The twelve northern states operating sharia criminal law for Muslims (Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara) sit outside this southern state, so the death penalty exposure documented under those regimes does not reach a visitor to Abia. The federal penalties and the national arrest climate, however, apply in full.

A 2022 federal court ruling struck down sections of the Act as unconstitutional, but the core offences and penalties remain in force. The UK government's June 2025 country-policy note documents tens of LGBT+ arrests per year nationally, alongside police harassment including beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture. A visitor to Abia is exposed to this federal enforcement posture from the point of entry.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern of enforcement includes mass arrests at social venues and police stops based on perceived presentation, documented across multiple Nigerian states between 2018 and 2023. Abia has no separately documented incident of this kind in the sources, but the federal law underpinning such stops applies statewide.

At least four sharia death sentences have been imposed in northern states since 2022, none carried out. This is context for the wider Nigerian legal environment a visitor passes through en route to Abia, not a risk specific to this state.
localsOnly:
Residents of Abia live under the same federal SSMPA framework as visitors, with the additional exposure of being subject to routine policing rather than entry-point screening. The 2022 federal court ruling striking down sections of the Act as unconstitutional offers limited but real constitutional protection against its most expansive readings, though the core offences remain.

LGBTQ Nigerians nationally report lost job prospects, reluctance to seek medical care or report crimes, and chilled access to HIV prevention services as a direct consequence of the Act. These are resident-facing burdens that a short-term visitor is less likely to encounter but a resident of Abia faces as a matter of daily life.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Abia-specific arrest, prosecution, or incident of anti-LGBT violence is documented in the source inventory. The state-level enforcement picture is unresolved on the available sources; the assessment rests on the federal framework and national patterns.

The practical scope of the 2022 federal court ruling striking down sections of the SSMPA is not specified in the sources — which sections were invalidated, and whether that ruling has been appealed or narrowed, remains not sourced here.

Whether Abia State has any local ordinance addressing cross-dressing or gender presentation, distinct from the federal framework, is not sourced.
